title: Create, save and inspect a valid HTML document
learningObjectives: Create a correctly named .html file in a predictable project directory and distinguish it from a rich-text document.
Construct a standards-mode HTML document using the doctype declaration and the html, head and body elements.
Set the document language, character encoding, responsive viewport metadata and a meaningful page title.
Explain the difference between metadata in the head and visible document content in the body.
Open a local HTML document in a browser and distinguish file editing from browser rendering.
Use the browser's developer tools to inspect the parsed DOM and diagnose common file, path and markup mistakes.
Explain why valid nesting, explicit document structure and meaningful titles matter for maintainability and accessibility.

understand.concept: An HTML document is a text resource that a browser parses into a document tree. A practical project begins with a predictable folder and a file saved with the .html extension. A complete modern document declares the HTML standard mode, identifies the document language, provides essential metadata in the head, and places the page's content in the body. The browser does not display the source file as plain text by default; it parses the markup and constructs a DOM representation.
understand.whyItMatters: A reliable document shell prevents avoidable problems with character encoding, mobile viewport sizing, page titles, language identification and script/style loading. It also gives later lessons a stable place to add semantic content, CSS and JavaScript.
understand.history: The doctype declaration is a document-level instruction that helps browsers use standards mode. Modern HTML uses a short doctype rather than the longer declarations associated with older HTML versions.
understand.analogy: Think of the document as a structured data file with a defined root and separate metadata and content sections.
understand.analogyLimit: The browser is not simply opening a text file and showing each line. It tokenizes and parses markup, builds a DOM, applies CSS and may execute scripts; malformed markup can be repaired according to parsing rules.

explain.narrative: Create a folder such as web-project and save the file as index.html using a code editor that saves plain text. Avoid accidental names such as index.html.txt. Open the file in a browser, then use View Source to inspect the original text and Developer Tools → Elements to inspect the DOM the browser constructed. These are related but not identical views. Keep metadata in head and user-facing page content in body. The lang attribute identifies the primary language of the document and helps assistive technology and language-aware tools. UTF-8 supports a broad range of writing systems. The viewport metadata allows the layout viewport to match the device width; it does not itself make a layout responsive.

examples.explanation: The title appears in browser chrome such as the tab, not as a visible heading inside the page. The h1 and paragraph are body content.

examples.title: Check the actual file extension
examples.code:
Correct:   index.html
Incorrect: index.html.txt
Incorrect: index.htm.html.txt
examples.explanation: Some operating systems hide known file extensions. Check the complete file name when a browser displays markup as text or opens an unexpected file.
examples.expectedOutput: The file name ends in .html exactly once.

practise.guidedTask: Create a new folder named html-document-lab and add index.html. Reproduce the complete document example, change the title and heading, save the file, and reload it in the browser. Then compare View Source with the Elements panel and identify the html, head, title, body and main nodes.
practise.independentTask: Create a two-page local project with index.html and about.html. Give each page a distinct title, correct lang attribute, UTF-8 declaration and viewport metadata. Add a working relative link between the pages. Inspect both pages at a narrow viewport and confirm that the browser is loading the files you edited.
hints: Use a plain-text code editor. A word processor may insert formatting that is not valid source code.
Check the complete file name, including hidden extensions, if the browser does not open the expected page.
Keep title and metadata in head; place visible content in body.
Use one meaningful h1 for the primary page heading as a useful default, but do not treat heading levels as a visual sizing tool.
View Source shows the source text; the Elements panel shows the parsed and potentially modified DOM.
The viewport meta tag establishes the layout viewport. Responsive CSS rules are still required for a responsive layout.

questions.prompt: Which element contains the document's primary visible content?
questions.explanation: The body contains the document content rendered as part of the page. The head contains document metadata and resource references.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the UTF-8 charset declaration?
options: To make every layout responsive automatically.
To declare the character encoding used to interpret the document text.
To load the page's CSS file.
questions.answer: To declare the character encoding used to interpret the document text.
questions.explanation: The charset declaration helps the browser decode text correctly. It does not control layout or load stylesheets.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between View Source and the Elements panel?
options: View Source shows source text; Elements shows the browser's parsed DOM, which scripts may later modify.
Elements displays only CSS and never HTML.
questions.answer: View Source shows source text; Elements shows the browser's parsed DOM, which scripts may later modify.
questions.explanation: The DOM is the browser's in-memory document representation and can change after the original response is loaded.

questions.prompt: Does the viewport meta tag alone make a page responsive?
options: Yes, it creates all breakpoints automatically.
No, responsive layout still requires suitable CSS and flexible content.
Yes, but only on desktop browsers.
questions.answer: No, responsive layout still requires suitable CSS and flexible content.
questions.explanation: Viewport metadata establishes the intended layout viewport. CSS must still adapt the layout to available space.
